questions.text: A public library has 800 sqm of reading/study areas. Using the RA 9514 2019 Revised IRR, calculate the occupant load for these areas.

rationale.a: Uses the outdated or incorrect factor of 4.6 sqm (intended for laboratories).
rationale.d: This is the floor area, not occupant load.
rationale.correct: Per RA 9514 2019 IRR Table 10.2.7.3.1, 'Classrooms' and 'Reading Rooms' have an occupant load factor of 1.9 sqm/person (net). 800 sqm ÷ 1.9 ≈ 421.05, which rounds up to 422.

questions.text: A library contains 600 sqm of reading area and 400 sqm of open-shelf stacks. Using RA 9514 2019 IRR factors, calculate the total occupant load.

rationale.a: Uses 4.6 factor for reading and 9.3 for stacks.
rationale.c: Uses 1.9 factor for the entire area.
rationale.correct: 1. Reading Area: 600 sqm ÷ 1.9 = 316 occupants. 2. Stacks: 400 sqm ÷ 9.3 = 43 occupants. Total = 316 + 43 = 359 occupants.

questions.text: A school library must serve 600 students according to DepEd standards. What is the minimum required floor area for the library facility?

rationale.correct: DepEd Educational Facilities Manual specifies 1.5 sqm per student for library spaces. 600 students × 1.5 sqm = 900 sqm.

questions.text: A municipal library serves 30,000 residents. According to PRC Standards, what is the recommended floor area range?

rationale.correct: PRC standards for public libraries: 10,000–50,000 residents require a 500–1,500 sqm facility.
rationale.takeaway: Library size is categorized by population served: 10k-50k = 500-1,500 sqm.

questions.text: Why is the occupant load factor for library reading areas (1.9 sqm/person) significantly denser than general business offices (9.3 sqm/person)?

options.text: Libraries have higher fire risks due to paper storage, which necessitates stricter safety measures and denser occupancy
Library activities (reading/study) are stationary and seated at high-density tables/carrels, whereas offices require more circulation space per employee.
Offices are Group E and libraries are Group A-2, which affects the calculation of occupant load factors based on different usage types
The factor for libraries is based on the number of books, not the area, which leads to a different approach in determining space requirements

rationale.a: Fire risk determines building construction type, not occupant load density.
rationale.c: Occupancy group is a result of use, not the cause of the density factor.
rationale.d: Factors are strictly area-based in the Fire Code.
rationale.correct: Occupant load factors reflect physical density. Seated study (1.9) is dense; office work (9.3) involves desks, equipment, and circulation, allowing for fewer people in the same area.
rationale.takeaway: Higher density (1.9) = Seated stationary; Lower density (9.3) = Office/Business.

questions.text: Under PD 1096, what occupancy group classification applies to a public library?

options.text: Group E (Business/Mercantile), which typically includes spaces used for the transaction of business or the rendering of professional services.
Group C (Education and Recreation), which covers facilities primarily used for educational purposes and recreational activities.
Group A-2 (Institutional branch libraries and museums)
Group H (Assembly/Public Gathering), which is designated for buildings used for assembly purposes, including theaters and lecture halls.

rationale.a: Group E is for commercial offices and retail; libraries are institutional.
rationale.b: Group C is strictly for schools and educational institutions.
rationale.d: Group H is for assembly buildings with fixed seating or high-density stages.
rationale.correct: PD 1096 Rule VII Table VII.1 explicitly classifies 'branch libraries and museums' as Group A Division 2. This is a common ALE trap where students mistake it for Group C (Educational).
rationale.takeaway: Public Libraries = Group A-2. Schools = Group C.

questions.text: A research library vault for manuscripts maintains 18–21°C and 45–55% RH. How should this non-public storage be treated for occupant load?

options.text: Excluded from building occupancy as it is a restricted support space.
Calculated as Reading Room at 1.9 sqm/person.

rationale.a: Incorrect; all areas contribute to the total building load for egress sizing, even at low densities.
rationale.d: Vaults are not for general business staff activities.
rationale.correct: RA 9514 Section 10.2.1.2 requires every building part to be calculated. Even if non-public, storage/warehouse areas use the factor of 27.9 sqm/person.

questions.text: A library has 900 sqm reading, 400 sqm stacks, and 200 sqm admin offices. What is the total building occupancy load?

rationale.a: Uses incorrect factors for reading room.
rationale.c: Uses a single factor for the entire building area.
rationale.takeaway: Sum individual occupancy loads for each functional space type.

questions.text: A school library serves 800 students. Based on DepEd and Fire Code requirements, is a single 1.0 m wide door adequate for the facility?

options.text: Yes, 1.0 m meets the minimum door width for any room.
No, the calculated occupant load is 632; minimum 3 exits are required.
No, the calculated occupant load is 632; required width is 3,160 mm.
Yes, if the travel distance to the next exit is less than 30 meters.

rationale.a: Minimum width is met, but aggregate width is not.
rationale.b: Correct that 3 exits are required for 501-1,000 persons, but the primary failure is the width.
rationale.d: Travel distance is a separate requirement from exit capacity.
rationale.correct: 1. Area = 800 students × 1.5 sqm = 1,200 sqm. 2. Occupancy = 1,200 ÷ 1.9 = 631.5 ≈ 632. 3. Width (Level/Door) = 632 × 5.0 mm = 3,160 mm. One 1,000 mm door is inadequate.
rationale.takeaway: Check: 1. Minimum individual width, 2. Aggregate width, 3. Number of exits.

questions.text: A university library is designed for 2,174 occupants. Using RA 9514 2019 IRR, what is the required aggregate exit width for the stairs?

rationale.b: Uses the level component/ramp factor (5.0 mm).
rationale.correct: Exit width for stairs is 7.6 mm per person. Calculation: 2,174 × 7.6 = 16,522.4 mm, rounded to 16,523 mm.
rationale.takeaway: Stair Width Factor = 7.6 mm/person; Level Component Factor = 5.0 mm/person.
